edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: A snap election in Spain, questions over security at a UK airbase and a major Danish data breach lead today’s coverage.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and substantial public-interest reporting. Related coverage of the same events is grouped; reports and allegations remain attributed where facts are unsettled.

content.headline: Spain’s Sánchez calls snap election after housing reforms are defeated
content.shortHeadline: Spain heads for snap election after housing vote defeat
content.standfirst: Pedro Sánchez has called a general election for 29 November after parliament rejected two government housing measures. Protests over rents and evictions have intensified pressure on his minority coalition.

image.caption: Pedro Sánchez’s announcement followed the defeat of housing measures in parliament.

sources.originalTitle: Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests

segments.body: Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said Spain will vote on 29 November, earlier than planned, after lawmakers defeated two decree laws intended to protect tenants. He said he needed a broader progressive majority to advance reforms. The election had been expected by summer 2027 at the latest.

segments.title: Housing at the centre of the campaign
segments.body:
The defeats came amid protests in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona. Anger grew after 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her Madrid home following a sharp rent increase; her lawyer says she will be able to return. The proposed measures included suspending some evictions and extending certain rental contracts, but opponents argued intervention could reduce rental supply and push prices higher.

Sánchez’s Socialists govern with junior coalition partner Sumar but lack a parliamentary majority. The opposition People’s Party won the most seats in the 2023 election but fell short of governing alone; most opinion polls cited in the report suggest it may again need support from the hard-right Vox party.

content.headline: Nobel medicine prize honours discoveries that let scientists control brain cells
content.shortHeadline: Nobel prize recognises discoveries that illuminate brain circuits
content.standfirst: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the prize for work behind optogenetics, a method that uses light to switch specific neural circuits on or off. Researchers are exploring possible medical applications.

image.caption: The Nobel Committee announced the medicine prize at the Karolinska Institute in Sweden.

sources.originalTitle: Nobel Prize awarded for revealing inner workings of the brain

segments.body: The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine has been awarded to US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and German researchers Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. Their work helped establish optogenetics, allowing scientists to use light-sensitive proteins to control the electrical activity of nerve cells.

segments.title: From laboratory tool to possible treatment
segments.body:
Hegemann and Nagel discovered channelrhodopsin, a protein found in algae; Deisseroth worked out how to use it to switch nerve cells on and off in mice. Researchers have since used the technique to study brain circuits and their links to memories, feelings and behaviour.

Clinical research is also under way to restore some vision in people with retinitis pigmentosa by introducing a light-sensitive protein into a damaged part of the eye. The report describes this as an early step towards treatment, not an established cure.

content.headline: Two crew members reported dead after strike sinks cargo ship in Black Sea
content.shortHeadline: Cargo ship sinks after Black Sea strike; accounts of casualties differ
content.standfirst: Ukraine says a Russian drone attack sank a Turkish-owned vessel carrying corn in neutral waters. Romania reported two deaths, while Ukraine’s president said the captain was killed and another sailor was missing.

image.caption: Romanian authorities reported a fire aboard a vessel outside their territorial waters.

sources.originalTitle: Zelensky condemns 'horrific' Russian strike on boat carrying corn in Black Sea

segments.body: Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said two drones struck the Royad Mammadov, a civilian vessel carrying corn, and that 11 crew members were rescued. He said the captain was killed and another sailor was unaccounted for. Romania said two people had died after a fire on the ship, which it located in its exclusive economic zone, about 30 nautical miles south of Sfantu Gheorghe.

segments.title: A contested and widening maritime conflict
segments.body:
Russia has not commented on the reported attack. Its defence ministry had earlier said it struck two cargo vessels. Russia says its strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure are retaliation for Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries and ships; Kyiv says its attacks target infrastructure that helps finance the war.

Zelensky said Ukraine had proposed steps to reduce tensions and protect Black Sea security. He called for pressure to safeguard global food security. The report does not establish the precise location of the strike or resolve the differing accounts of the deaths.

content.headline: Yemen’s government says forces have retaken ground near Bab al-Mandab
content.shortHeadline: Yemen government claims gains near strategic Bab al-Mandab
content.standfirst: Pro-government forces say they have secured the area around the strategic Red Sea strait as a new offensive begins. Houthi-run media deny government advances, and the conflict has displaced nearly 200,000 people since August, according to the UN.

sources.originalTitle: Yemeni government forces say they have 'secured' Bab al-Mandab Strait

segments.body: Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia say they have taken control of an airport near Dhubab and cut a road to the port city of Mokha. A military spokesman said the forces were besieging Houthi fighters in the coastal town, which overlooks the Bab al-Mandab Strait. Houthi-run media deny government forces have advanced there.

segments.title: Renewed fighting and a fragile truce
segments.body:
Yemen’s internationally recognised leadership announced an offensive to retake territory held by the Houthis, while a Saudi-led coalition said its aircraft had hit more than 300 targets. The Houthis have also claimed attacks on Saudi oil sites. These are competing claims from parties to the conflict; the report does not independently verify territorial control.

The war began in 2014 and escalated the following year with Saudi-led intervention. An informal ceasefire that had lasted four years began to unravel in July. The government’s health ministry says 959 people have been killed and 5,000 injured since 6 August; the UN says 197,000 people have been displaced.

content.headline: French school protests grow after teenager loses hand in Lens confrontation
content.shortHeadline: France school protests widen after teenager loses hand
content.standfirst: A 15-year-old was seriously injured during a protest in Lens as demonstrations over school conditions spread. The circumstances of his injury remain disputed, and an investigation has been opened.

image.caption: Police face a protesting student outside a secondary school in Bordeaux.

sources.originalTitle: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
France braces for national day of school protests as boy loses hand

segments.body: A 15-year-old boy lost a hand during a confrontation near a school in Lens, northern France. The prefect said the teenager’s life was not in danger and that he was taken to hospital. Reports differ on whether he picked up a police stun grenade before it exploded; the town’s mayor said the circumstances still needed to be clarified. A regional prosecutor said the police watchdog would investigate.

segments.title: Disputes over schools and policing
segments.body:
The protests began over conditions including staff shortages and deteriorating buildings. France’s prime minister has asked ministers to address pupils’ demands, including replacing absent teachers and proposing repairs to school buildings. A trade union leader said limited measures would not satisfy protesters and criticised budget cuts and the police response.

The Guardian reports that thousands were expected to join a national day of demonstrations, while the education minister said hundreds of schools were partly or fully closed. Its account also reports a separate complaint from the family of a pupil who lost sight in one eye after an earlier protest; an investigation is under way.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s reporting adds the government’s response on school staffing and repairs, and criticism from the CGT union, which argues the proposed steps do not meet the scale of pupils’ grievances.

content.headline: Flydubai co-pilot accused of planning to crash plane into Tel Aviv target
content.shortHeadline: Flydubai co-pilot accused of planning attack on Tel Aviv flight
content.standfirst: The UAE says a co-pilot tried to seize a Dubai-to-Tel Aviv flight after attacking the captain with a crash axe. Reports say he intended to crash the plane, but investigators have yet to establish the full circumstances or motive.

image.caption: Captain Smit Machchhar was seriously injured in the alleged attack aboard the flight.

sources.originalTitle: Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say
Six things to know as Flydubai pilot used ‘axe in attempted terrorist attack’

segments.body: The UAE attorney-general says the co-pilot of Flydubai flight FZ1073 attempted a terrorist act on the flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. He allegedly attacked and wounded the captain with a crash axe before passengers overpowered him. Another crew member was able to land the plane in Saudi Arabia; the suspect remains under investigation in the UAE.

segments.title: Investigators examine motive and security checks
segments.body:
US and Israeli media reports, citing people familiar with the investigation, say the co-pilot told investigators he intended to crash the aircraft into Ben Gurion airport or a building in Tel Aviv. Those reported intentions have not been confirmed by Emirati or Israeli authorities, who say the investigation is continuing.

The captain described fighting to open the cockpit door despite his injuries, and passengers said they helped subdue the co-pilot. The reports also raise questions about hiring and security screening: officials told media that Oman had barred him from flying over concerns about extremist views. The full details of his recruitment and vetting remain unclear.

perspectives.body: The i Paper adds accounts from the injured captain and passengers about how they regained access to the cockpit, as well as flight-tracking details from the incident.

content.headline: Nigerian police say explosives are delaying rescue of 19 abducted recruits
content.shortHeadline: Suspected explosives delay rescue of 19 abducted recruits
content.standfirst: Police say drones located a camp in Imo state where 19 youth service recruits are being held, but fear it is mined. Families say kidnappers are demanding ransom; authorities have not identified those responsible.

image.caption: Omotosho Adewale says his child is among the recruits abducted in Imo state.

sources.originalTitle: Bombs preventing rescue of kidnapped youths, Nigerian police say

segments.body: Nigerian police say they have located a camp where 19 National Youth Service Corps recruits abducted last week are being held. Police Commissioner Audu Bosso said drones helped find the site, but officers believe it is mined with homemade explosives. Bulldozers and armoured vehicles are being deployed as a rescue operation is prepared.

segments.title: Families await news
segments.body:
The recruits were travelling from Ibadan to orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states when gunmen attacked their buses near Umunoha in Imo state. Omotosho Adewale, whose child is among those abducted, told the BBC that a ransom of 50 million naira had been demanded. He said he had not eaten for three days from worry.

Police have not disclosed the camp’s location or identified the kidnappers. Authorities have not linked the abduction to any group. The incident has renewed concern about travel risks for young people taking part in the compulsory national service programme.

content.headline: US marine arrest renews Okinawa residents’ anger over military presence
content.shortHeadline: Murder arrest revives Okinawa anger over US military presence
content.standfirst: A US Marine is in Japanese custody after police arrested him in connection with the death of a woman in Okinawa. Residents say the case has revived longstanding grievances about crimes and the concentration of US bases on the island.

sources.originalTitle: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa

segments.body: Japanese police arrested US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard in connection with the death of 39-year-old Anna Yagi, whose body was found in a Naha hotel room. Police say the investigation is continuing. The suspect is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was not related to official military duties.

segments.title: Longstanding local opposition
segments.body:
The arrest has prompted protests in Naha and Tokyo and renewed calls from Okinawa residents for concrete action. The island hosts the largest US military presence in Japan, including tens of thousands of personnel. Local opposition has been shaped by past crimes, accidents, noise and aircraft crashes.

The report says Okinawa Prefectural Government records 6,409 arrests for criminal offences related to US military personnel since the prefecture returned to Japanese control in 1972. Those figures describe a long history of local concern; they do not establish the facts of the current case.

content.headline: US withdraws bombers from RAF Fairford amid reported new security threat
content.shortHeadline: US pulls bombers from RAF Fairford after reported new threat
content.standfirst: The US has returned its bombers from Gloucestershire to American bases after reports of fresh warnings about a possible Iran-backed plot. British authorities say RAF Fairford is safe, but the reason for the withdrawal has not been fully confirmed.

image.caption: A US B-1 Lancer bomber takes off from RAF Fairford.

sources.originalTitle: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base
US bombers pulled from RAF Fairford base after suspected terror plot
All the signs that Iran was behind RAF Fairford ‘terror plot’
Why US bombers departing RAF Fairford could mark new chapter in Iran war

segments.body: The Pentagon confirmed that all US bombers deployed at RAF Fairford had returned to their home stations. US media reported that commanders received new details about a possible Iran-backed threat to the base. Six men have been arrested in connection with an investigation into events around Fairford and later released on bail; no explosives were found in the search described by the Guardian.

segments.title: What is known about the decision
segments.body:
Downing Street says the base is safe and declined to comment on another country’s military operations. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he would not directly link the withdrawal to the earlier incident, described movements of military assets as normal, and said the US had confidence in its bases and British cooperation. The BBC reports that UK officials do not dispute that the withdrawal was connected to the incident, but say it was an operational military decision.

Iran has denied involvement in the alleged plot. Police investigations continue, and the available reporting does not establish the nature of the latest warning or who, if anyone, was behind it.

perspectives.body: The i Paper cites analysts who differ on the implications: some see a precaution to protect scarce aircraft, while another says a reduced US presence in Europe or strains with the UK cannot be ruled out.

content.headline: Rachel Jupp appointed director of BBC News as broadcaster faces trust challenges
content.shortHeadline: Rachel Jupp takes charge of BBC News amid trust and AI challenges
content.standfirst: The former Panorama editor will lead BBC News after Deborah Turness’s departure over the editing of a Donald Trump speech. Jupp takes over as the BBC faces job cuts and questions about impartiality, audience trust and the use of AI.

image.caption: Rachel Jupp has been appointed director of BBC News.

sources.originalTitle: BBC appoints Rachel Jupp as new director of news
Former Panorama editor Rachel Jupp appointed as head of BBC News

segments.body: Rachel Jupp has been appointed director of BBC News, nearly a year after Deborah Turness resigned following the controversy over a Panorama edit of a speech by Donald Trump. Jupp previously worked at Newsnight and edited Panorama. She has also led BBC work on generative AI and, most recently, news documentaries and long-form journalism.

segments.title: A newsroom under scrutiny
segments.body:
Jupp will oversee about 4,500 staff as the BBC plans sweeping savings: around 550 news job closures have been announced, while the corporation expects to cut between 1,800 and 2,000 jobs overall. The BBC says it faces significant financial pressures.

The Guardian reports that Jupp’s recent work included addressing editorial issues after a BBC documentary about children in Gaza breached accuracy guidelines by not disclosing the narrator’s family connection. It also cites a Reuters Institute figure putting UK trust in news at 30%, down 20 percentage points from a decade ago. Jupp says she wants to strengthen trust in the BBC’s journalism.

perspectives.body: The Guardian adds detail on editorial controversies beyond the Trump edit and on Jupp’s role in the BBC’s AI strategy, highlighting the breadth of scrutiny facing her new newsroom.

content.headline: Police data show thousands of sexual offences against children recorded at UK
content.shortHeadline: Police record thousands of sexual offences against children at school
content.standfirst: Guardian analysis found an average of 4.7 reported sexual offences against under-13s a day on or near school premises in England and Wales from 2021 to 2025. Campaign groups are urging the government to act, while the data does not identify the alleged perpetrators in most cases.

image.caption: The reported offences were recorded on or near school premises in England and Wales.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham urged to ‘end cycle of harm’ after scale of child-on-child sexual abuse revealed

segments.body: Police recorded at least 8,500 sexual offences against children under 13 as occurring on school premises or nearby in England and Wales between 2021 and 2025, according to Guardian analysis of police data. That is an average of 4.7 reported offences a day. The analysis includes almost 2,000 reports of rape or attempted rape; most records did not specify the alleged perpetrator’s age.

segments.title: Calls for action
segments.body:
A letter signed by 87 academics and campaign organisations urges Prime Minister Andy Burnham to take decisive action on violence against women and girls. The signatories say the recorded cases are only part of the picture because much abuse goes unreported, and point to earlier reviews and calls for change.

The report says lawyers and experts believe fellow pupils are likely to be responsible in many cases, but the police figures do not establish that for each offence. The Department for Education was contacted for comment.

content.headline: SEND support plan faces staffing shortages, councils warn
content.shortHeadline: Staff shortages threaten promised SEND support in schools
content.standfirst: The government’s £1.8bn Experts at Hand scheme aims to bring specialist help into mainstream schools, but at least 36 councils have raised concerns about finding enough staff. Ministers say the phased rollout is under way and recruitment will take time.

image.caption: Schools minister Georgia Gould promoted the Experts at Hand scheme at Labour conference.

sources.originalTitle: SEND pupils’ extra support at risk with schools unable to access specialist staff

segments.body: Schools may struggle to provide specialist support promised under the Experts at Hand scheme because of shortages of educational psychologists, speech and language therapists, occupational therapists and specialist teachers. At least 36 councils have raised staffing concerns, according to analysis by Schools Week. The programme, launched last month, has £1.8bn in funding over three years.

segments.title: Capacity remains the test
segments.body:
Councils including Hertfordshire and Cheshire West and Chester warned that a lack of a national workforce strategy and difficulties recruiting specialists could undermine delivery. A charity leader said she had not received firm plans from any of the 20 councils it works with. A 2025 Education Policy Institute report estimated that nearly 100 council areas needed another 1,400 full-time-equivalent educational psychologists.

The Department for Education said the scheme is being rolled out in phases and that local areas need time to recruit and build capacity. School leaders and support organisations warn that children may wait for help if specialists are not available.

content.headline: Scotland’s proposed AI data centres raise energy, water and planning concerns
content.shortHeadline: Scotland weighs costs and promises of a data-centre boom
content.standfirst: At least 23 large data centres are proposed in Scotland, with supporters promising investment and jobs. Campaigners and experts question their demand for power and water, while ministers have declined to impose a moratorium.

image.caption: A Google data centre in Cheshunt, Hertfordshire.

sources.originalTitle: Why are data centres such a big deal in Scotland?

segments.body: Scotland is part of a race to build large data centres to support artificial intelligence. One proposal at Chapelcross could reach 1,000 megawatts, while the planned Auchtertool site in Fife would cover 60 hectares. Supporters point to investment and employment; critics say the scale could put pressure on local communities and the environment.

segments.title: Power, water and local planning
segments.body:
Scotland’s wind resources are a selling point for developers, but the report cautions that this does not mean centres would run entirely on renewable electricity: fossil-fuel power may be needed when wind and solar generation are low. Large facilities may also use substantial water for cooling, and residents elsewhere have reported persistent fan noise.

The Scottish government has rejected a call for a moratorium and says environmental assessments will be required. Ministers say new guidance is expected before Christmas and that approval for large schemes before then is highly unlikely.

content.headline: Student housing failures leave some UK accommodation blocks empty
content.shortHeadline: Student housing squeeze deepens as costly blocks struggle
content.standfirst: The collapse of a Dundee student accommodation operator left nearly 70 students searching for rooms, while some purpose-built blocks elsewhere have low occupancy. High rents, rising costs and uneven demand are exposing pressure across the market.

image.caption: Purpose-built student accommodation blocks are facing financial pressure and uneven demand.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I didn’t know what to do’: collapse of providers of high-end digs leaves students in shock

segments.body: Nearly 70 students in Dundee had to find new accommodation after the owner of Marketgait Apartments went bust in July. The case is part of a broader squeeze: some purpose-built student accommodation blocks are struggling as construction and borrowing costs rise, international student numbers fall in some markets and rents outpace many students’ means.

segments.title: A mismatch between supply and affordability
segments.body:
Demand varies sharply between cities. In Nottingham, the number of students seeking beds fell from a pandemic-era peak while thousands of additional purpose-built rooms entered the market. Providers are concentrating on cities with stronger universities and some are reducing rents, selling sites or considering other uses for rooms.

For many students, the bigger problem is affordability: maintenance loans have not kept pace with rents, and some students rely on family support, share private flats or commute. The National Union of Students says some students are becoming homeless or relying on food banks; it argues that accommodation needs better regulation and lower costs.

content.headline: Experts warn public ownership alone will not fix Avanti’s rail problems
content.shortHeadline: Avanti nationalisation will not quickly fix delays or fares
content.standfirst: Avanti West Coast is due to return to public ownership in March, but experts say its worst delays stem largely from capacity and infrastructure problems on the West Coast Main Line. They caution that nationalisation is no guarantee of cheaper fares.

image.caption: Avanti West Coast had the lowest on-time performance of UK rail operators last year.

sources.originalTitle: The UK’s worst rail firm is being nationalised. But don’t expect improvements soon

segments.body: Avanti West Coast had the lowest on-time performance of UK operators in 2025–26, with 37.9% of trains on time, and the second-highest cancellation rate, according to the Office of Rail and Road. The government says the operator will return to public ownership, but rail experts warn that the change alone will not resolve the underlying causes of disruption.

segments.title: Infrastructure and fares
segments.body:
Network Rail problems accounted for 66% of Avanti’s delayed minutes, the regulator’s figures show. Experts describe the West Coast Main Line as congested, with capacity bottlenecks that require investment to fix. A £400m programme of signalling and track work is under way, but one expert says it is largely maintenance rather than a major expansion of capacity.

Public ownership could make coordination between the operator and Network Rail easier, experts say, but they do not expect it to bring fares down without additional public funding. The government has not committed to cheaper tickets.

content.headline: Study links problematic social media use to health risks for under-25s
content.shortHeadline: Study links problematic digital media use to health risks
content.standfirst: A Lancet series analysing reviews covering nine million people under 25 found links between problematic digital media use and mental health, sleep and exercise. Researchers say the evidence is not conclusive but warrants action and greater platform transparency.

image.caption: Researchers examined possible health risks linked to digital media use by people under 25.

sources.originalTitle: Three ways social media is harming young people, according to landmark study

segments.body: A three-paper series in The Lancet links problematic digital media use among under-25s to higher risks of mental health problems, sleep difficulties and reduced exercise. The researchers reviewed evidence covering nine million people. They describe the associations as modest and say they are not conclusive; the findings do not establish that screen use alone causes these outcomes.

segments.title: Calls for scrutiny of platform design
segments.body:
Researchers argue that features such as infinite scrolling, autoplay and personalised recommendation feeds should be examined, and say companies should share more data for independent research. They also called for coordinated action by governments. Some policy experts favour regulating specific platform features rather than relying only on age bans.

The report says the findings are likely to intensify debate in the UK, where a ban for under-16s is due to take effect from March next year. Enforcement and the consequences of such bans remain contested.

content.headline: Personal data of 8.8 million people exposed in Danish CPR breach
content.shortHeadline: Danish CPR breach exposes data on 8.8 million people
content.standfirst: Unauthorised users accessed names, addresses and CPR numbers by misusing a company’s legitimate access to Denmark’s civil register. Authorities say protected names and addresses were not included; the method and those responsible remain unknown.

image.caption: Names, addresses and CPR numbers belonging to about 8.8 million people were compromised.

sources.originalTitle: Uvedkommende har haft adgang til 8,8 millioner CPR-numre
Professor: 'Det største brud nogensinde mod det danske CPR-register'
Styrelse melder om forsinket hjemmeside og travlhed efter CPR-læk

segments.body: Unauthorised users obtained access to names, addresses and CPR numbers for about 8.8 million registered people after misusing a Danish company’s authorised access to the Central Person Register, the responsible ministry says. The register holds about 11 million records, including those of people who have died or moved abroad. The company’s access has been stopped and the incident reported to the data protection authority.

segments.title: Risks and investigation
segments.body:
A cybersecurity professor called it the largest breach of the CPR register to date and warned that the combination of addresses and CPR numbers could make phishing and identity theft more convincing. The minister says authorities are still mapping the full extent of the incident. Police have opened a high-priority investigation; how access was obtained and who was responsible remain unknown.

Authorities advise people to be alert to unexpected calls, emails or texts asking for passwords or MitID details. The Digitalisation Agency said high traffic delayed its register-insight website, and the cyber-security hotline extended its weekday opening hours.

content.headline: Most Danish dementia patients wait beyond legal deadline for assessment
content.shortHeadline: Dementia assessment waits exceed Denmark’s legal limit for most
content.standfirst: A National Audit Office review found that about 84% of patients were not assessed within the legal 30-day limit from 2022 to 2025. The average wait in 2025 was at least 165 days, delaying access to treatment and support.

image.caption: Denmark’s public auditors criticised regions over delays in dementia assessments.

sources.originalTitle: Lange ventetider til udredning for demens møder kritik: De fleste bliver ikke udredt inden for reglerne

segments.body: About 24,960 people referred for a dementia assessment between 2022 and 2025 did not receive one within 30 days, the National Audit Office says. That represents about 84% of patients in the review. The average assessment wait in 2025 was 165 days or more than five times the legal limit.

segments.title: Pressure on regional services
segments.body:
The auditors say long waits increase the risk that patients receive appropriate treatment and support too late. Denmark’s public auditors issued a sharp criticism of the regions, the second-highest level of criticism they can make. The health minister has four months to respond.

The chair of Danish Regions acknowledged that the criticism was justified and said services need to be reorganised to assess more people, potentially with general practitioners taking on a greater role. The government has announced 680 million kroner over four years for a dementia plan, but the report says a detailed plan has not yet been presented.

content.headline: Salling Group buys online retailer Proshop in billion-kroner deal
content.shortHeadline: Salling Group buys Proshop to expand its online business
content.standfirst: The owner of Bilka, Føtex and Netto is acquiring a majority stake in Danish online retailer Proshop in a billion-kroner transaction. Proshop will keep its brand and founder Poul Thyregod will remain chief executive.

image.caption: Salling Group is acquiring a majority stake in Aarhus-based online retailer Proshop.

sources.originalTitle: Salling shopper igennem: Køber dansk netbutik i milliardhandel

segments.body: Salling Group has agreed to buy a majority stake in Aarhus-based online retailer Proshop, in what its chief executive calls the group’s second-largest acquisition. He would not disclose the price, but said it was a billion-kroner deal. Proshop reported revenue of almost 4.5 billion kroner last year.

segments.title: A push into online retail
segments.body: Salling Group says the purchase will strengthen its online business in electronics and toys, and that it hopes to learn from Proshop’s e-commerce expertise. The company says Proshop will continue under its own brand, with founder Poul Thyregod remaining as managing director. Proshop employs more than 350 people.

content.headline: Fyn police acknowledge failures after neighbour’s call before woman’s death
content.shortHeadline: Police change call-handling rules after missed response before death
content.standfirst: Police did not attend after a neighbour twice reported worrying sounds from a 23-year-old woman’s flat. Fyn Police say they should have told him when they decided not to send a patrol; her family says a different response might have saved her.

image.caption: Cecilie Voller Kjærulff died in her flat in Odense.

sources.originalTitle: Nabo ringede forgæves: Politiet erkender fejl i sag om 23-årigs død

segments.body: Cecilie Voller Kjærulff, 23, was found dead in her Odense flat the day after her neighbour called police twice about unusual sounds. An autopsy concluded she probably died from an overdose of medication prescribed for bipolar disorder, with alcohol, MDMA and cocaine also found in her blood. The neighbour says he was told police would come, but no patrol arrived.

segments.title: New procedures after review
segments.body:
Fyn Police say the decision not to attend was based on the information available at the time, but acknowledge that the caller should have been told the patrol would not come. The force says it has tightened call-centre procedures and reinforced guidance on asking questions.

Experts in poisoning told DR they believe she would probably have survived if she had reached hospital when the neighbour called. Her parents are critical of the police response; the police inspector says the neighbour did what he could and responsibility lay with the force to ask the right questions.

content.headline: Denmark drops 40-day target for first meeting in high-conflict divorces
content.shortHeadline: Delayed family meetings leave parents and children waiting
content.standfirst: More than 80% of high-conflict divorce cases missed the target for a first meeting with the Family Court Agency within 40 days last year. The agency says it now contacts families earlier, but lawyers warn that long waits can deepen disputes.

image.caption: Families in high-conflict divorce cases have faced long waits for a first meeting with the agency.

sources.originalTitle: Alarm om børn i skilsmissekaos: Hjælpen kommer for sent

segments.body: The Family Court Agency no longer has a target requiring parents in difficult divorce cases to be called to a first meeting within 40 days. DR’s records request found that the target was missed in more than 80% of such cases last year, with delays increasing. These cases can involve suspected violence, mental illness and deep mistrust between parents.

segments.title: Concerns about children and due process
segments.body:
A family sociologist at VIVE says prolonged waiting can increase stress and allow conflict to escalate, including situations where one parent loses contact with children. The Danish Association of Family Lawyers criticised dropping the target, saying people should be told how long they will wait.

The agency says cases accumulated during the introduction of a new IT system and changes to working practices. It says staff now speak to parents earlier and offer advice before the first meeting, with a focus on the child.

content.headline: Hunters search Rømø for invasive rodent that could damage sea defences
content.shortHeadline: Invasive rodent prompts hunt to protect Rømø’s dykes
content.standfirst: A nutria has been sighted several times on Rømø, where hunters are trying to remove it before it burrows into the island’s protective dykes. Seven nutrias were recorded in Denmark this year, up from two last year.

image.caption: A hunter waits in an area on Rømø where a nutria has been seen.

sources.originalTitle: På vadehavsø jagter de invasiv gnaver: 'Den er en stor trussel'

segments.body: Regulated hunters are searching for a nutria on Rømø after it was first spotted in early September. The invasive rodent digs burrows in banks and dykes, raising concern on an island where earthen defences protect residents from storms and flooding. Hunters have not yet caught the animal.

segments.title: More sightings reported
segments.body: Nutrias originate in South America and were brought to Europe for fur farming. Authorities recorded seven in Denmark this year, compared with two last year, and say the animals are arriving from Schleswig-Holstein, where they have an established population. National Park Wadden Sea staff warn the numbers could grow if the animals are not controlled.

content.headline: Copenhagen committee considers ending permit for Aarhus seaplane route
content.shortHeadline: Copenhagen vote could end Aarhus seaplane route
content.standfirst: The city’s environment and technology committee is considering whether to renew the permit for the Aarhus–Copenhagen seaplane, which carried about 13,000 passengers last year. Officials have recommended against renewal, and the airline says it may have to close if it cannot land in the capital.

image.caption: The seaplane serving Aarhus and Copenhagen is pictured in Copenhagen harbour.

sources.originalTitle: Den hurtigste rute mellem Danmarks to største byer risikerer at miste livet i dag

segments.body: Nordic Seaplanes has linked Aarhus and Copenhagen by air for about ten years, with a flight time of roughly 45 minutes. Copenhagen’s environment and technology committee is due to consider the route’s future. City officials have recommended that its environmental permit not be renewed, and a majority of the committee is reported to be ready to end it.

segments.title: Convenience versus environmental impact
segments.body:
The airline’s director says losing permission to land in Copenhagen after the end of the year could force the company to close. Last year the service carried more than 13,000 passengers, with one-way fares ranging from 699 to 2,200 kroner.

A Copenhagen politician opposing renewal says a fossil-fuel aircraft does not belong in the city harbour, particularly with an airport nearby. The airline says a central landing point is important to passengers and that sheltered harbour water is necessary for safe operations.

content.headline: Skive restaurant choice sparks dispute over lack of labour agreement
content.shortHeadline: Skive challenged over royal visit to restaurant without agreement
content.standfirst: A municipal choice of restaurant for King Frederik and Queen Mary’s visit has drawn criticism because the venue has no collective agreement. The mayor says the meal will go ahead there, citing its location near a site the royals are due to open.

image.caption: King Frederik and Queen Mary are due to visit Skive during the town’s anniversary celebrations.

sources.originalTitle: Kongeparret er inviteret på restaurant uden overenskomst: Politiker kalder det forkert

segments.body: Skive Municipality has invited the king and queen to a meal at Hereford Beefstouw during the town’s 700th-anniversary celebrations. A local SF councillor says the municipality should set an example by choosing a restaurant with a collective agreement. The restaurant says negotiations for a new agreement have broken down.

segments.title: The municipality defends its choice
segments.body:
The mayor says the meal will remain at the restaurant, which is near the Fjordbadet bathing facility the royal couple are due to inaugurate. He argues that the municipality cannot require a restaurant to have a collective agreement and says he plans to meet the 3F union.

The councillor says she is not making a claim about the restaurant’s actual working conditions, but argues the municipality should be certain those conditions are in order. The restaurant and royal household had not responded to DR’s requests for comment.

content.headline: Metallica’s Sphere residency turns a rarities set into an immersive epic
content.shortHeadline: Metallica turn Sphere rarities set into an immersive epic
content.standfirst: The band opened its Las Vegas residency with a no-repeat promise and a set spanning decades. The Sphere’s monstrous visuals sometimes compete with the music, but a tight, forceful performance holds its ground.

image.caption: Metallica perform at Sphere in Las Vegas.

sources.originalTitle: Metallica review – metal titans on fine form in spectacular rarities-focused show

segments.body: Metallica launched their 24-show Life Burns Faster residency with a set designed to reward dedicated fans: the band say they will play twice a week without repeating a song within the same week. Rather than rely on a greatest-hits sequence, the opening night moved across their catalogue, from “Now That We’re Dead” and “Lux Æterna” to “The Call of Ktulu” and “Seek and Destroy”.

segments.title: The band against the spectacle
segments.body: The Sphere’s enormous images turn songs into theatrical scenes: during “The Call of Ktulu”, a giant creature stalks a projected Las Vegas; for “Ride the Lightning”, the audience sees the action from an electric chair. At times the scale overwhelms, but the review finds the group’s playing—especially Lars Ulrich’s fluid drumming and James Hetfield’s voice—keeps the show focused.

content.headline: Liz Harris finds a restorative counterpoint to Grouper’s solitude in Helen
content.shortHeadline: Liz Harris finds restoration in Helen’s shared sound
content.standfirst: The ambient musician discusses the return of her dream-pop trio and the relief of making music with friends. A viral track also brought a stark lesson in how easily streaming royalties can be stolen.

image.caption: Liz Harris of Helen and Grouper.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s rational to fear the music industry’: Grouper’s Liz Harris on virality, streaming scammers and her ‘restorative’ dream-pop trio

segments.body: Liz Harris describes Grouper as intensely solitary music, but says the revived trio Helen lets her show a more playful, social side. Making Helen’s new album, Linda’s Head, was “really restorative” while she was dealing with medical difficulties. Its collaborative brightness does not erase the darkness in the songs; it gives that darkness company.

segments.title: The risks of sudden attention
segments.body: Harris says a fraudulent upload of her song “Poison Tree” accrued millions of plays and around six figures before she and her label were able to stop the scam and recover what she was owed. Fake remixes and tracks with matching titles have also required constant attention. The experience, she says, has reinforced her fear of becoming more deeply involved in the music industry.

content.headline: Tom Morello’s first solo rock album turns protest into a family legacy
content.shortHeadline: Tom Morello brings protest and family into solo debut
content.standfirst: On Everyone Gets What They Want, the Rage Against the Machine guitarist renews his political call to action and works with his teenage son. He traces that conviction to his mother, Mary, whose example shaped his activism.

image.caption: Tom Morello during an interview about his new solo album.

sources.originalTitle: Tom Morello on Rage Against the Machine fans turning against him

segments.body: Tom Morello calls Everyone Gets What They Want his first full-length solo rock album, a collection of anti-racist and anti-fascist songs that he describes as a “call to arms”. It features Serj Tankian, Kneecap and Morello’s 15-year-old son Roman, who co-wrote five tracks. Morello says making rebellious music feels like self-care in a dangerous time.

segments.title: A conviction learned at home
segments.body: Morello credits his mother, Mary, with teaching him that ordinary people can change the world. He recalls her taking part in civil-rights and anti-colonial causes and explaining why their family would join the United Farm Workers grape boycott. After her death at 102, he set up a memorial project encouraging people to donate, volunteer and protest in causes she supported.

content.headline: Interpol revisit their New York roots and widen their sound on This Mirror Weigh
content.shortHeadline: Interpol revisit New York and widen their sound
content.standfirst: The band’s eighth album brings fresh arrangements to their familiar angular indie rock. Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler discuss a return to recording in New York, the band’s early scene and their wariness about AI-made art.

image.caption: Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler of Interpol.

sources.originalTitle: Interpol: ‘People romanticise the Noughties music scene. We weren’t all friends’

segments.body: This Mirror Weighs a Ton is presented as a return to form with new textures: ambient and trip-hop elements, piano ballads, woodwind and, for the first time on an Interpol track, acoustic guitar. The band recorded in Manhattan with producer Andrew Wyatt, and bassist Brad Truax joined the writing process as a full member.

segments.title: The scene, remembered differently
segments.body: Paul Banks and Daniel Kessler recall the much-romanticised New York indie scene of the early 2000s with some reservations. Banks says he once pushed back against the idea that its bands were all friends; Kessler recalls wanting to find like-minded peers but rarely seeing that sense of camaraderie. They also argue that artists seek sincerity and expression, not music made merely to be sold.

perspectives.body: Kessler says Interpol’s return to writing in New York brought a sense of history and belonging. Banks, meanwhile, links the new album’s themes to modern life, including war footage he encountered online and questions about how language shapes truth.

content.headline: Soft Cell’s Danceteria becomes a final album after Dave Ball’s death
content.shortHeadline: Soft Cell’s final album closes a long creative partnership
content.standfirst: Marc Almond says he and Dave Ball had finished Danceteria just two days before Ball died in 2025. The album revisits their early-80s New York years, mixing dance-pop exhilaration with memories of a scene later transformed by AIDS.

image.caption: Marc Almond and Dave Ball of Soft Cell.

sources.originalTitle: Soft Cell’s Marc Almond: ‘We finished the album – two days later Dave passed away’

segments.body: Soft Cell’s sixth album, Danceteria, is also their last: Marc Almond says he would not make another record under the band’s name without Dave Ball. The pair agreed the album was finished, Almond recalls, two days before Ball died in his sleep at 66 in October 2025, after years of health problems.

segments.title: A city in the music
segments.body: The album looks back to the New York clubs that changed Soft Cell, with Almond describing a world that was dangerous, dark and creatively exuberant. Tracks evoke the rush of nightlife but also its loneliness and the way the city changed as AIDS took its toll. Almond says he felt relief that he and Ball had made the record together, even as he mourns that Ball would not see its release.

content.headline: Jake Xerxes Fussell turns old folk fragments into a coherent, wandering album
content.shortHeadline: Jake Xerxes Fussell makes old songs feel newly travelled
content.standfirst: The North Carolina musician draws on traditional ballads, blues and sea shanties for a subdued record of drifters and uneasy travellers. The review finds a strikingly unified album in those far-flung sources.

sources.originalTitle: The Old Beloved Path

segments.body: On The Old Beloved Path, Jake Xerxes Fussell builds most of the songs from traditional material, from an Irish ballad to a blues standard. His plaintive baritone and fingerpicking sit among harmonica, mandolin and fiddle, with production by Ben Whiteley. The review describes a meditative record that makes an unusually coherent whole from diverse sources.

The songs gather people in motion: sailors, drifters and others looking for a new beginning. Fussell’s “Boll Weevil” turns a familiar blues figure into a dispossessed wanderer, while “Rock Island Line” combines an old nursery rhyme with the skiffle song, becoming a slow-moving travel tune. The review’s point is that these old routes can still lead somewhere unexpected.

content.headline: Elvis Costello’s expanded My Aim Is True traces a gradual transformation
content.shortHeadline: A Costello box set reveals the slow making of My Aim Is True
content.standfirst: The 104-track anniversary edition revisits the making of Costello’s debut, with demos and live recordings that complicate the idea of an overnight breakthrough. The review hears a craftsman finding his voice over time.

sources.originalTitle: My Aim Is True (49th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new five-CD edition of My Aim Is True adds demos, live sets and earlier recordings to Elvis Costello’s 1977 debut. Rather than simply celebrating a finished classic, the collection tracks an artist trying out influences and approaches. Its second disc, The Blue Print, is especially revealing: the songs show a capable writer before the punk and new wave character of the album had fully emerged.

segments.title: A voice taking shape
segments.body: The review describes the album’s blend of catchy complaint-rock, musical range and sharp writing, with “Alison” still its emotional centre. Later discs follow Costello’s songs and persona coming into sharper focus, while the final Clover reunion recording is judged more a fan’s keepsake than an essential chapter. Together, the set makes the case for gradual transformation rather than sudden invention.

content.headline: The Beatles’ Rubber Soul remains an album of productive contradictions
content.shortHeadline: Rubber Soul’s many versions keep the Beatles classic in flux
content.standfirst: The new deluxe set gathers UK and US editions, alternate mixes and studio outtakes around a record that changed pop’s sense of what an album could be. The review argues there is no single definitive version.

sources.originalTitle: Rubber Soul (Super Deluxe)

segments.body: Rubber Soul marked a shift toward the Beatles treating an album as an artwork in its own right, while they were still racing to meet a release deadline. The new set documents that compressed process through alternate takes, mixes and recording notes. Its UK and US editions also reveal how label decisions produced different versions of the same landmark record.

segments.title: No one real Rubber Soul
segments.body: The review finds pleasure in the set’s contrasts: stereo and mono, the UK and US tracklists, finished songs and outtakes. Small details in the mixes can alter the feel of a performance, but the new remix is not a wholesale reinvention. The larger point is that the album has never been one fixed object; listeners bring their own history to the version they know.

content.headline: Digger’s box-office failure sharpens the debate over Tom Cruise’s climate satire
content.shortHeadline: Digger flops as critics split over Cruise’s climate satire
content.standfirst: Alejandro G Iñárritu’s film opened to $20m worldwide against reported production and marketing costs far higher. Critics disagree over whether its deliberately awkward performance and theatrical reveal add up to an audacious work or a failed experiment.

image.caption: Tom Cruise as Digger Rockwell and Riz Ahmed as Dr Nirav Ganesh in Digger.

sources.originalTitle: Digger may lose $150m after Tom Cruise film bombs at the box office
Tom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpiece
Tom Cruise has forgotten how to act
Digger review: Tom Cruise takes the 'biggest risk of his career' in this 'love-it-or-hate-it' folly ★★★★☆

segments.body: Digger took $20m globally in its opening weekend, including $8m in North America, according to the box-office report. Its production budget has been reported at between $125m and $150m, with marketing estimated at a further $100m; one projection put the potential loss at about $150m. The weak debut follows a heavily criticised release and leaves the film far short of its awards-season ambitions.

segments.title: A reveal that divides critics
segments.body: The film’s central twist reframes Tom Cruise’s oil tycoon as an actor performing in a play about climate catastrophe. One critic argues the reveal makes Digger a sharp question about art, reality and the limits of satire; another finds Cruise’s performance too self-conscious to persuade. The BBC review calls the film an eccentric, politically blunt folly and praises its ambition, while acknowledging its excesses.

perspectives.body: The BBC review embraces Digger as a risky, conceptually challenging eco-satire, arguing that Cruise’s commitment and the film’s environmental message make its excesses worthwhile.

content.headline: Sense and Sensibility’s new adaptation prompts debate over Austen’s heroines
content.shortHeadline: A new Sense and Sensibility puts Austen’s heroines in focus
content.standfirst: Georgia Oakley’s film brings fresh attention to Elinor and Marianne, while critics and experts debate what screen versions gain—and lose—when they emphasise romance, looks and visual atmosphere over Austen’s social observation.

image.caption: Daisy Edgar-Jones as Elinor Dashwood in Georgia Oakley’s adaptation.

sources.originalTitle: Every millennial should read Sense and Sensibility
Fiona Shaw: ‘They didn’t think women were funny when I was young’
'The 21st-Century gym-toned bodies put me out': Four things Jane Austen adaptations get wrong - according to experts

segments.body: The new Sense and Sensibility, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles, is darker and less glossy than the much-loved 1995 version, according to the review. Its story of two sisters negotiating money, love and social expectations also invites a modern reading: the tension between guardedness and emotional excess still feels familiar in a culture shaped by public sharing and uncertain prospects.

segments.title: What adaptations can leave behind
segments.body: A discussion with Austen specialists argues that adaptations can make romance the main event at the expense of class and women’s financial insecurity, while modern beauty standards and reduced dialogue can flatten the novels’ subtleties. Fiona Shaw, who plays Mrs Jennings, describes Oakley’s approach as pared back; she also sees her character as performing a role while remaining essentially benign.

perspectives.body: The experts’ criticism is not a demand for literal fidelity: they focus on what screen versions may lose when Austen’s irony, conversational detail and social critique give way to romantic imagery.

content.headline: Comédie Française turns backstage Macbeth chaos into a brisk French farce
content.shortHeadline: Comédie Française makes pre-show Macbeth chaos funny
content.standfirst: A run of mishaps threatens to derail opening night, leaving the director to take over as Lady Macbeth. The review praises the performers’ comic timing while finding the film’s career-and-motherhood subplot less convincing.

image.caption: A scene from Comédie Française.

sources.originalTitle: Comédie Française review – pre-show bedlam plays theatrical chaos for laughs

segments.body: The film unfolds in the three hours before a Paris production of Macbeth is due to open. Its director, Nina, arrives without her staff pass and faces a mounting list of problems: missing performers, superstitious actors, technical obstacles and an absent Lady Macbeth. The review calls the French farce a hoot, especially as Nina is forced to consider stepping into the role herself.

The comic mayhem includes a stoned grande dame, rehearsal-time infidelity and a stage manager who explains in exhaustive detail why each problem cannot be solved. The review finds the cast’s timing and its portrait of theatrical egos consistently enjoyable, though it is less persuaded by the subplot about Nina balancing motherhood with her career.

content.headline: Behemoth! lets a gifted cello player drift through an unfocused drama
content.shortHeadline: Behemoth! is undone by its wandering structure
content.standfirst: Tony Gilroy’s first feature in years has an intriguing musical setting and a strong cast, but its shifting timelines, subplots and styles leave the film without a compelling centre, according to the review.

image.caption: Pedro Pascal in Behemoth!.

sources.originalTitle: Behemoth! review - Pedro Pascal classical music drama hits all the wrong notes

segments.body: Pedro Pascal plays Alex, a cello virtuoso who returns to Los Angeles for session work and to be near his family. He is haunted by a past affair with a violinist and becomes preoccupied with her daughter, a teenage musical prodigy. The review sees promise in the premise and the film’s musical world, but says a disorienting structure prevents its parts from coming together.

segments.title: A drama without an anchor
segments.body: The film moves from grief and yearning to action scenes, with flashbacks and subplots that the review finds insufficiently developed. Eva Victor’s performance is singled out as a bright spot, while Pascal’s Alex is judged too distant from his own life to hold the story together. The result, in the critic’s view, is a film that gestures toward weighty themes without making them resonate.

content.headline: The Yellow Tie follows a conductor who insisted music must be heard live
content.shortHeadline: The Yellow Tie profiles a conductor opposed to recordings
content.standfirst: John Malkovich plays Sergiu Celibidache in a family-directed biopic about the celebrated conductor’s refusal to record music. The review finds a sturdy, heartfelt film, though it questions the force of its central argument.

image.caption: John Malkovich in The Yellow Tie.

sources.originalTitle: The Yellow Tie review – John Malkovich gives major hauteur as legendary record-hating maestro

segments.body: Sergiu Celibidache believed recorded music was inert and that a performance mattered because it happened in the moment. The Yellow Tie follows his rise from a young musician in Nazi-era Berlin to principal conductor of the Berlin Philharmonic after the war, and then through a wandering career across Europe and Latin America.

Directed by Celibidache’s son, the film is described as robust and heartfelt, with John Malkovich playing the older conductor and Ben Schnetzer the younger one. The review sees a lonely heroism in Celibidache’s insistence on live performance, but wonders what the film makes of a position that gathered few followers in a music world full of equally principled musicians who disagreed.

content.headline: Karl Lagerfeld’s public persona still eludes this authorised documentary
content.shortHeadline: Karl Lagerfeld remains elusive in a dutiful documentary
content.standfirst: Nick Hooker’s film draws on the designer’s biography and access to people around him, but the review finds that it rarely gets beneath his carefully managed image or examines his controversies in depth.

image.caption: Karl Lagerfeld in his signature style.

sources.originalTitle: Karl review – straightforward tribute tells inside story of fashion world’s great eccentric Karl Lagerfeld

segments.body: Karl draws on William Middleton’s biography and interviews with Lagerfeld’s inner circle, alongside archive footage. It recalls his reinvention of Chanel and his later celebrity, while acknowledging how closely he guarded his private self. The review says that access to associates does not necessarily reveal the man behind the dark glasses and carefully delivered wit.

The documentary’s most revealing testimony comes from long-serving collaborators, including seamstress and adviser Amanda Harlech, rather than Lagerfeld’s famous friends. The review also notes that a brief reference to his controversial fatphobic comments is quickly passed over. It judges the film diligent but not definitive.

content.headline: James Dean’s fame hid the vulnerable young actor behind the icon
content.shortHeadline: Remembering the vulnerable actor behind James Dean’s icon
content.standfirst: A close reading of Dean’s brief career looks beyond the rebellious image to a performer frightened by sudden fame. His most affecting screen moment, the review argues, is one of need rather than cool.

image.caption: James Dean on the set of Giant in 1955.

sources.originalTitle: The truth about James Dean

segments.body: James Dean’s three leading film roles came in a career cut short by his death at 24. The article traces his work with director Elia Kazan, who drew on Dean’s strained relationship with his father when shaping Cal in East of Eden. It also considers how comparisons with Marlon Brando obscured the differences in their acting styles.

Dean’s image as a photogenic rebel was amplified after his death, but the piece argues that his vulnerability remains visible in East of Eden. Its final example is the unscripted moment when Cal embraces his father after a rejection: rather than the cool icon, the article sees a desperate young man reaching for affection.

content.headline: The Reluctant Vampire makes Eric Morecambe’s children’s books a family comedy
content.shortHeadline: The Reluctant Vampire is a comic treat for all ages
content.standfirst: Lenny Rush leads a warm, joke-packed adaptation about a human boy raised by vampires. The review praises its ensemble and the writing team’s affection for Morecambe’s books; Rush sees the story as a comic take on belonging.

image.caption: Lenny Rush as Valentine in The Reluctant Vampire.

sources.originalTitle: The Reluctant Vampire review – Lenny Rush’s absolute joy of a comedy is perfectly cast
Fangs a million: Lenny Rush on turning an Eric Morecambe classic into a hilarious vampire comedy

segments.body: Valentine is the second son in a vampire family, but he has no fangs, dislikes blood and cannot fly. The truth is that Valeeta rescued him as a human baby and brought him up as her own. The six-part adaptation of Eric Morecambe’s children’s books follows the family’s efforts to conceal that secret, with a new friendship adding to Valentine’s complicated life.

segments.title: Comedy with a sense of belonging
segments.body: The review celebrates Lenny Rush’s performance and a supporting cast that includes Tom Davis, Sian Clifford, Bill Bailey and Ross Noble. Rush describes the story as a universal teenage struggle to fit in, despite its vampires and gargoyles. He also says the show is intended for everyone, not only children.

perspectives.body: Rush sees Valentine’s difference as a metaphor for wondering whether you are doing things right or are good enough. He says hearing from families whose disabled children felt encouraged by his work has been a welcome, unexpected effect.

content.headline: Richard E Grant’s Traitors blunder and Ross Kemp’s paranoia set an unruly tone
content.shortHeadline: A Traitors confession and Ross Kemp’s nerves shake the castle
content.standfirst: Richard E Grant told a fellow player he was a Traitor almost as soon as he was chosen, while Ross Kemp turned innocent gestures into signs of danger. The opening episode’s mistakes may be just what makes this celebrity series compelling.

image.caption: Richard E Grant in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: Richard E Grant has already ruined The Celebrity Traitors. It’s brilliant
Ross Kemp’s Traitors paranoia will be the Faithfuls’ downfall

segments.body: Richard E Grant’s apparent slip came moments after he and Maya Jama were chosen as Traitors: asked directly by Joe Lycett, Grant said he was one. The review reports that the producers and players were left unsure whether it was a blunder or a double bluff. It concludes that the confession’s confusion gives the new series an unusually dramatic launch.

segments.title: Suspicion can turn inward
segments.body: Ross Kemp, a Faithful, suspects Bella Ramsey after a harmless gesture and then worries that Leigh-Anne Pinnock has marked him for murder. The accompanying analysis argues that his vocal paranoia risks drawing attention and spreading false leads among the Faithful. It also notes the Traitors’ decision to use Kemp in a mission that could make him look suspicious.

perspectives.body: The analysis reads Kemp’s anxious play as a possible response to his tough public image: he may fear being humiliated, but saying every suspicion aloud is making him look more vulnerable.

content.headline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after its latest revival stalls
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who faces an uncertain future after its latest revival
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, cancelled a planned Christmas special and has no current Doctor. Fans and former contributors disagree on what went wrong, but hope the long-running series can return without losing its core values.

image.caption: Illustrations of several Doctor Who incarnations, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Doctor Who has been off screen since its 2025 series, and the BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+. A planned Christmas special has been cancelled, the show has no current Doctor, and the corporation is seeking a new funding partner. No one has yet stepped forward, leaving the series’ immediate future unclear.

segments.title: What comes next?
segments.body: The article traces the show’s past revivals and reinventions, from its 2005 return to the contested casting of its most recent Doctors. Contributors raise different concerns: Frank Skinner wants the BBC to act faster, while writer Nina Metivier points to the show’s traditions of kindness and curiosity. Others question whether scripts and the funding strategy served the programme.

perspectives.body: Skinner argues that Doctor Who did not need a huge Disney+ investment simply to tell a good story and worries about how long it has been kept off air. Scriptwriter Nina Metivier describes kindness and curiosity as values at its core.

content.headline: Friday Night Lights made small-town Texas football a story about people
content.shortHeadline: Friday Night Lights found humanity beyond the football field
content.standfirst: Twenty years on, the drama’s improvisational style, ensemble and close sense of place still stand out. Its world was shaped by a book about the costs and expectations surrounding high-school football in Texas.

image.caption: Connie Britton and Kyle Chandler in Friday Night Lights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Brave from the beginning’: 20 years of Friday Night Lights – the sports drama that dared to be different

segments.body: Set in Dillon, Texas, Friday Night Lights centred on high-school football but drew on H. G. Bissinger’s reporting about Odessa and the pressures surrounding the sport. The series showed a town where games shaped the week, while also reflecting the racism, strained school resources and broken ambitions described in the book.

segments.title: A naturalistic ensemble
segments.body: Director Peter Berg encouraged actors to improvise and used handheld cameras, helping conversations feel less scripted. The show also gave its women characters lives beyond football and launched or advanced careers including Jesse Plemons and Michael B. Jordan. Despite narrative missteps, the article argues, its humanity and precise sense of place kept it grounded.

content.headline: The Split-Up brings a British Asian family into the centre of a glossy legal
content.shortHeadline: The Split-Up puts a British Asian family at its centre
content.standfirst: The Manchester-set spin-off carries forward The Split’s family and divorce-court drama with a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Its creators describe that everyday representation as a deliberate choice.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split-Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split-Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister preparing to take over her family’s Manchester firm, until her mother’s death changes her father’s succession plans. A former partner joins the firm, and the six-part series pairs divorce cases with conflict inside the family. Ritu Arya says the role felt like a full-circle moment after growing up inspired by Goodness Gracious Me.

segments.title: Representation as ordinary life
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living everyday lives rather than being defined by exceptional circumstances. Executive producer Abi Morgan says the spin-off keeps the original’s focus on family, love and betrayal while giving a new writing team room to shape it. Arya also describes researching the work of family lawyers for her role.

perspectives.body: Sarma says the series could not represent every part of British Asian culture; her aim was to create one family she recognised as contemporary and real, rather than a token version of a whole community.

content.headline: 70 Up ends a decades-long portrait of lives—and the camera’s influence
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up closes a life-spanning documentary experiment
content.standfirst: The final chapter of the series begun as Seven Up! revisits its participants and the choices that shaped their lives. It also makes space for criticism from some contributors about the way director Michael Apted portrayed them.

image.caption: Participants in the Seven Up! documentary series as children.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: The series began in 1964 by asking 14 seven-year-olds from different backgrounds what they thought their futures might hold. It returned to many of them every seven years, following changes in work, family and circumstance. With 70 Up, producers say, the experiment reaches its intended ending rather than continuing until only one participant remains.

segments.title: Who controls the portrait?
segments.body: The finale revisits criticism that the series’ interviews and editing sometimes narrowed participants into types. Peter Davies says he left after tabloid attacks on his comments about Margaret Thatcher, then returned years later partly to promote his writing and music. Others questioned whether Apted’s questions reflected assumptions about class and gender; the producer argues the participants and programme maintained trust.

perspectives.body: Davies says he is glad to have taken part but notes that there is always more to a person than a few hours of television can show. He does not feel sadness about the series ending and thinks it is the right time.

content.headline: Nigella Lawson’s Bake Off judging offers a welcome rejection of food guilt
content.shortHeadline: Nigella Lawson brings unapologetic pleasure to Bake Off
content.standfirst: The new judge’s delight in biscuits and objection to calling food “naughty” make a pointed contrast with calorie-conscious food talk. The review sees her approach as a refreshing presence on mainstream television.

image.caption: Nigella Lawson judges on The Great British Bake Off.

sources.originalTitle: Nigella is dismantling skinny culture one ‘naughty cookie’ at a time

segments.body: Nigella Lawson has brought an unguarded enjoyment of food to The Great British Bake Off, the review argues. When fellow judge Paul Hollywood described a contestant’s cookies as “naughty”, Lawson objected: “I don’t approve of talking about food as naughty. We need to take our pleasures where we can in life.”

The article contrasts Lawson’s approach with a wider culture of calorie counting and weight-loss marketing, and with the language of whether a treat is “worth the calories”. It argues that her visible pleasure in baking and eating offers a welcome alternative, while making clear that this is the writer’s response to her role on the show.

content.headline: Damilola Taylor’s story gets a moving account from people who knew him
content.shortHeadline: A new film honours Damilola Taylor through those who knew him
content.standfirst: Friends, family and people involved in the case revisit the killing of the ten-year-old and its aftermath. The programme also asks why similar deaths occurred, holding onto grief while finding room for hope in his legacy.

image.caption: Damilola: The Untold Story on BBC Two.

sources.originalTitle: TV tonight: an essential film about the story of Damilola Taylor

segments.body: Damilola: The Untold Story brings together people who knew the ten-year-old, including actor John Boyega and his sister Grace, who were with Damilola at the library shortly before his death. His brother Tunde and caretaker Guillermo Casal also revisit the events that led to the conviction of two brothers.

The television recommendation describes the programme’s trauma and sadness as palpable, but says it also finds love and hope in Damilola’s legacy. It broadens its view from the case to ask why there were so many similar killings, while giving those closest to him the chance to tell their account.

content.headline: Gears of War: E-Day’s excellent combat can’t save a repetitive prequel
content.shortHeadline: Gears of War: E-Day has thrilling combat but little else
content.standfirst: The prequel returns to the series’ alien invasion and delivers its most satisfying combat in years. But recycled routes, overstuffed maps and disruptive collectibles make the surrounding campaign feel safe and drawn out.

image.caption: Marcus Fenix in Gears of War: E-Day.

sources.originalTitle: Gears of War: E-Day review – an alien invasion shouldn’t be this boring

segments.body: E-Day depicts the invasion that has haunted the Gears of War series, with Marcus Fenix and a mismatched squad caught in a city under attack. Its best passages revive the horror and grimness of the early games, while the combat feels better than ever: movement is more natural, cover more fluid and firefights richly destructive.

segments.title: The campaign runs out of road
segments.body: The review finds the level design repetitive, sending players over the same ground in different conditions and filling large areas with collectibles and side objectives. A nearby-item chime can even cut across an emotional scene. The fighting remains a strength, but the game around it does not build on its early ideas.

content.headline: Resident Evil’s new film recreates the fear of playing the games
content.shortHeadline: Resident Evil finds horror in the experience of playing
content.standfirst: Zach Cregger leaves familiar heroes off screen and follows an ordinary courier through a world of scarce ammunition, cryptic clues and escalating danger. The result, this feature argues, adapts the games’ mechanics as much as their mythology.

image.caption: Director Zach Cregger on the set of Resident Evil.

sources.originalTitle: How Zach Cregger’s Resident Evil stands out from all other game adaptations

segments.body: The film’s protagonist, courier Bryan Hodukavich, is thrust into a viral outbreak without weapons or a clear explanation. He moves through locations familiar from Resident Evil—an abandoned farmhouse, a tunnel, a hospital and a sewer—finding better weapons but rarely enough ammunition. Typewriters and brief encounters with other characters further echo the games.

segments.title: A player in an unfamiliar world
segments.body: Rather than retell a familiar hero’s story, the film draws on the vulnerability and uncertainty of playing: clues arrive through recordings and terse exchanges, and survival never feels guaranteed. The piece connects this approach to the game series’ design and argues that the film is still recognisably Resident Evil, even without its best-known characters.

content.headline: Ace Combat 8 delivers thrilling dogfights and an unexpectedly affecting story
content.shortHeadline: Ace Combat 8 soars on dogfights and an affecting story
content.standfirst: The aerial combat is fast, beautiful and varied, while more cinematic storytelling gives wingmates room to matter. Some busy battlefields are hard to read, and the reviewer could not test the brief multiplayer window.

image.caption: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve features aerial combat among striking cloudscapes.

sources.originalTitle: Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve review – brilliant aerial combat game fulfils the Top Gun fantasy

segments.body: Ace Combat 8 puts players in the role of a propaganda-invented ace pilot who becomes a real hero. Its dogfights are built for exhilaration rather than realism: intuitive controls help newcomers, while experienced players can use more demanding manoeuvres. Missions range from bombing runs to tracking radar-invisible aircraft, with dramatic radio chatter and music throughout.

segments.title: A more cinematic flight
segments.body: The review praises the game’s detailed skies, environmental destruction and new animated first-person scenes, saying the storytelling brings the pilot’s wingmates and their drama to life. Combat can become visually confusing, especially in cockpit view, and the multiplayer mode was available for only a short time during the review period, so the reviewer could not assess it.

content.headline: Roblox phishing scams trick children with promises of free Robux
content.shortHeadline: Fake Roblox logins put children’s Robux and data at risk
content.standfirst: Fraudsters use lookalike sign-in pages circulated through social platforms and gaming chats to steal account details. Security experts advise opening Roblox directly and treating authentication codes like passwords.

image.caption: Roblox advises users to access the service through its official app or website.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting children

segments.body: Scammers promise free Robux through links on YouTube, TikTok or Discord, then send players to fake sign-in pages that resemble Roblox. Children may enter passwords and two-factor codes before being redirected to the real service, leaving little obvious sign that their account details have been taken.

segments.title: How to reduce the risk
segments.body: NordVPN researchers say they found almost 200 addresses selling ready-made phishing pages over a seven-day period. The company advises families to open Roblox through its official app or website and never share authentication or backup codes. Roblox says it has security measures in place, but does not guarantee it can restore lost currency or items.

content.headline: A father and son replay the Call of Duty missions they never finished
